email.scenario: Rowley Regional Transit has announced that the last evening bus on route 9, which leaves the university at 10:40 p.m., will be dropped from the autumn timetable. The company has invited written comments from passengers before it makes a final decision next month. You depend on that bus after evening classes.
email.subject: Comments on the proposed route 9 timetable
bullets: Thank the company for inviting comments and say why the evening service matters to you.
Report a problem that dropping the last bus would cause for passengers like you.
Propose one alternative to cutting the service.

academicDiscussion.professorPost: When companies advertise an open position, some print the salary range in the posting itself, while others say only that the pay is competitive and leave the figure for a later conversation. Governments and employers in several countries are now debating whether that range should always appear in the advertisement. What do you think? Should employers be required to publish a salary range in every job posting? Why or why not?

studentPosts.name: Priya
studentPosts.post: Employers should have to publish it. Last summer I spent two weeks on an application and sat through two interviews, and only then did I learn that the pay would not cover my rent. The company knew that the whole time and I did not. That imbalance wastes the applicant's time, never the employer's.

studentPosts.name: Theo
studentPosts.post: In practice the rule produces ranges so wide that they tell an applicant nothing at all. It also creates problems inside the company, because employees who have worked there for years see a higher number advertised for their own job and quietly lose trust in their manager.
